newsitem.title: USA: Fed staff approach mixes science and "judgment".
newsitem.headline: Fed staff approach mixes science and "judgment".

text.p: Federal Reserve staffers use an array of sophisticated computer models to help chart the course of the economy, but ultimately their forecasts blend both art and science, Fed economists said Friday.

In a paper presented to the Carnegie-Rochester monetary policy conference here, they said computer models alone are insufficient for the analysis that is needed to set interest rate policy and that human judgement must also play a role.
"Economic analysis is both a science and an art," David Reifschneider, David Stockton and David Wilcox said.
"Science enters through the use of sophisticated econometrics, rigorous theory and high-speed computers," they said. "Art enters in order to deal with all the shortcomings of science. "
The paper discussed the role of computer models in the monetary policy process.
The Fed this year replaced its major model for analyzing the domestic economy, which had been in use since the 1960s, with an overhauled version.

The new model takes into account the economic expectations of financial market players, businesses and consumers as well as the impact of influences such as interest-rate changes and periodic swings in commodity prices.
In their article the Fed economists point out there is no one "official" model for the U.S. central bank.
"Rather," the authors said, "many models are in use, each designed with a different purpose in mind."

In addition to the new domestic model, the Fed has a large-scale model of the world economy and a model combining international and domestic equations. It also has a number of smaller models and relies on commercial models as well.
The detailed forecast the staff prepares for each Federal Open Market Committee meeting is a "judgmental" forecast that is not derived from a run of a major economic model.

Still, one important role for models is to examine the possible effects of monetary policy actions, the economists noted. They could also be used, for example, to determine the potential impact of a change in budgetary policies.

The Fed economists warned that use of a single model could lead to "straitjacket thinking" and might result in a situation where the staff might overlook important developments that could figure into the economic outlook.
Without some judgmental analysis, they added, a model might misinterpret the effects of unusual events such as strikes and natural disasters.
The models also cannot incorporate anecdotal evidence such as the information gathered from regional Fed banks for the periodic "Beige Book."
On the other hand, the economists said, relying on judgmental analysis alone has certain pitfalls, such as the potential for inconsistency.
The economists concluded an "eclectic" approach was the most useful and probably would be for the foreseeable future.
